section_1.title: Prerequisite: From Points to Directions
section_1.content: Briefly revisit the Cartesian coordinate system. Distinguish between a 'point' (a static location) and a 'vector' (an instruction for movement). Explain that while a point is a destination, a vector is the journey.
section_1.example: Imagine a cat sitting at coordinate (0,0). To get to a bowl of milk at (3,2), the cat must move 3 units right and 2 units up. That specific instruction—the movement itself—is our vector.

section_2.title: The Geometry of a Vector
section_2.content: Introduce the visual representation of a vector as an arrow in space. Emphasize two critical properties: Magnitude (length of the arrow) and Direction (where it points). Explain that vectors can slide around the graph as long as length and angle remain the same.
section_2.example: Visualize a gust of wind represented by an arrow. Whether the wind blows at the park or the beach, if it's 20mph heading North-East, it's the same vector.

section_3.title: The Algebra of Vectors: The 'Recipe'
section_3.content: Translate the visual arrow into a numerical list (a column matrix). Explain the [x, y] notation as a 'recipe' for movement. Show how the vector [3, -2] translates to '3 steps forward, 2 steps down' on the grid.
section_3.example: A game character 'Hero_A' has a movement vector of [4, 1]. In an animation, we show a ghost overlay of the hero moving 4 units along the x-axis and 1 unit up the y-axis to reach their new position.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_4.content: Demonstrate how to combine two vectors. Visually, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Numerically, show that we simply add the corresponding x and y components.
section_4.example: A plane is flying with a velocity vector [10, 0] (moving straight East). A crosswind hits it with a vector [0, 2] (moving North). The resulting path of the plane is the diagonal arrow formed by [10+0, 0+2] = [10, 2].

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World
section_5.content: Introduce 'Scalars' (regular numbers). Show how multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches, shrinks, or flips the direction (if the scalar is negative). This is the 'linear' part of linear algebra.
section_5.example: If a rocket's thrust vector is [1, 2], and we activate 'Turbo Mode' (a scalar of 3), the new vector becomes [3, 6]. Visually, the arrow grows three times longer but maintains the same slope.

section_6.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_6.content: Summarize how vectors serve as the building blocks for computer graphics, physics engines, and data science. Reiterate that a vector is both a geometric arrow and a list of numbers.
section_6.example: Show a quick montage: a 3D character model made of thousands of vectors, a weather map of wind velocities, and a search engine ranking results based on 'vector similarity'.

Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World

A scalar of two doubles the vector's length.
Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction.

lecture_lines: Vectors are both geometric arrows and numerical lists.

storyboard.title: The Geometry of a Vector

Every vector also points in a specific direction.

It remains the same if magnitude and direction persist.

section_2.title: The Geometry of a Vector
lecture_lines: Visually, we represent a vector as an arrow.
Every vector has a specific length, called magnitude.
Every vector also points in a specific direction.
You can slide a vector anywhere on the grid.
It remains the same if magnitude and direction persist.

section_3.title: The Algebra of Vectors: The 'Recipe'
lecture_lines: We write vectors as a list of numbers.
The numbers act as a recipe for movement.
Component x moves right; component y moves up.
animations: Display a column matrix [4, 1] in #FFFFFF text on the side of the screen.

Draw the resulting #FF4500 vector arrow over the traced path.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
lecture_lines: Adding vectors is like following sequential instructions.
Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.
The result is the arrow from start to end.
Numerically, we simply add the corresponding components.
This new vector represents the combined total movement.

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World
lecture_lines: Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors.
Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks the arrow.
A scalar of two doubles the vector's length.
Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction.
This scaling is the core of linear transformations.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: From Points to Directions", [
            "A point represents a static location in space.",
            "A vector is different; it represents movement.",
            "Think of it as a journey, not a destination."
        ])

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show a coordinate grid with a #FFFFFF dot at (0,0) labeled 'Cat'.
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        
        grid_plane = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-1, 5, 1],
            y_range=[-1, 5, 1],
            x_length=5,
            y_length=5,
            background_line_style={"stroke_opacity": 0.3}
        )
        self.place_in_area(grid_plane, 'A1', 'F6')
        
        cat_dot = Dot(color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(cat_dot, 'E2')
        
        cat_label = Text("Cat", font_size=20, color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(cat_label, 'F2') # Below Cat
        
        self.play(Create(grid_plane))
        self.play(FadeIn(cat_dot), Write(cat_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Fade in a #FFD700 dot at (3,2) labeled 'Milk'.
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        
        milk_dot = Dot(color="#FFD700")
        self.place_at_grid(milk_dot, 'C5')
        
        milk_label = Text("Milk", font_size=20, color="#FFD700")
        self.place_at_grid(milk_label, 'B5') # Above Milk
        
        self.play(FadeIn(milk_dot), Write(milk_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Draw a #00FF00 arrow starting at the 'Cat' and ending at 'Milk'.
        # Flash the #00FF00 arrow to emphasize the movement vector.
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        
        # Calculate arrow points using grid coordinates
        vector_arrow = Arrow(
            start=self.grid['E2'],
            end=self.grid['C5'],
            color="#00FF00",
            buff=0.1,
            stroke_width=6
        )
        
        self.play(Create(vector_arrow))
        self.play(Flash(vector_arrow, color="#00FF00", line_length=0.3))
        self.wait(2)

        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.4).scale(0.8)

        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Adjusting coordinates to fit the right side (0.5 to 5.5 range)
                x = 0.5 + j * 1.0
                y = 2.5 - i * 1.0
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):

        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section6Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary and Real-World Application", [
            "Vectors are both geometric arrows and numerical lists.",
            "They power physics engines, graphics, and data science.",
            "Mastering vectors unlocks the heart of linear algebra."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a vector field with multiple #FFFFFF arrows pointing in different directions.
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        
        arrows = VGroup()
        for i in range(4):
            for j in range(4):
                # Deterministic rotation for visual variety
                angle = (i * 0.7 + j * 1.3) % (2 * PI)
                arrow = Arrow(ORIGIN, 0.4 * RIGHT, buff=0, color="#FFFFFF", stroke_width=3)
                arrow.rotate(angle)
                arrow.move_to(np.array([i*0.8, j*0.8, 0]))
                arrows.add(arrow)
        
        self.place_in_area(arrows, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.9)
        self.play(LaggedStart(*[GrowArrow(a) for a in arrows], lag_ratio=0.05))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Highlight one arrow and transform it into a [x, y] column matrix.
        # Matching color for Line 2 and its matrix transformation.
        line2_color = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(line2_color))
        
        # Pick a central arrow to transform
        target_arrow = arrows[6] 
        
        # Pre-create matrix to avoid complex mobjects in updaters (though not using updaters here)
        matrix = MathTex(r"\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}", color=line2_color)
        self.place_at_grid(matrix, "C4", scale_factor=1.5)

        self.play(
            target_arrow.animate.set_color(line2_color).scale(1.2),
            *[FadeOut(a) for a in arrows if a != target_arrow]
        )
        
        self.play(Transform(target_arrow, matrix))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Show a simple #00FF00 wireframe mesh to represent a 3D model.
        line3_color = "#00FF00" # Green
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(line3_color))
        
        # Create a simple mesh-like structure
        mesh = VGroup()
        # Horizontal lines
        for i in range(6):
            l = Line([-1.5, i*0.5 - 1.25, 0], [1.5, i*0.5 - 1.25, 0], color=line3_color, stroke_width=1.5)
            mesh.add(l)
        # Vertical lines
        for i in range(6):
            l = Line([i*0.5 - 1.25, -1.5, 0], [i*0.5 - 1.25, 1.5, 0], color=line3_color, stroke_width=1.5)
            mesh.add(l)
        # Diagonal lines to give a 3D wireframe mesh aesthetic
        for i in range(5):
            for j in range(5):
                l = Line([i*0.5 - 1.25, j*0.5 - 1.25, 0], [(i+1)*0.5 - 1.25, (j+1)*0.5 - 1.25, 0], 
                         color=line3_color, stroke_width=0.8, stroke_opacity=0.6)
                mesh.add(l)

        self.place_in_area(mesh, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(target_arrow),
            Create(mesh, run_time=2)
        )
        self.wait(3)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Adding vectors is like following sequential instructions.",
            "Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.",
            "The result is the arrow from start to end.",
            "Numerically, we simply add the corresponding components.",
            "This new vector represents the combined total movement."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_PLANE = "#1E90FF"
        COLOR_WIND = "#FF00FF"
        COLOR_RESULTANT = "#FFFF00"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = YELLOW

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Introductory line
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR))
        self.wait(1.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw Plane and Wind vectors
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_WIND)
        )
        
        # Positions
        plane_start = self.grid["D2"]
        plane_end = self.grid["D4"]
        wind_start = plane_end
        wind_end = self.grid["B4"]
        
        # Plane Vector
        plane_vec = Arrow(plane_start, plane_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_PLANE)
        plane_label = Text("Plane", font_size=20, color=COLOR_PLANE)
        self.place_at_grid(plane_label, "E3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Wind Vector
        wind_vec = Arrow(wind_start, wind_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_WIND)
        wind_label = Text("Wind", font_size=20, color=COLOR_WIND)
        self.place_at_grid(wind_label, "C5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(plane_vec), Write(plane_label))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(Create(wind_vec), Write(wind_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Draw Resultant vector
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_RESULTANT)
        )
        
        res_vec = Arrow(plane_start, wind_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_RESULTANT)
        res_label = Text("Resultant", font_size=20, color=COLOR_RESULTANT)
        self.place_at_grid(res_label, "C2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(res_vec), Write(res_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Numerical addition
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(COLOR_RESULTANT)
        )
        
        # Math: [2, 0] + [0, 2] = [2, 2]
        math_addition = MathTex(
            r"\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}", 
            "+", 
            r"\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}", 
            "=", 
            r"\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}",
            font_size=32
        )
        # Apply colors to components
        math_addition[0].set_color(COLOR_PLANE)
        math_addition[2].set_color(COLOR_WIND)
        math_addition[4].set_color(COLOR_RESULTANT)
        
        self.place_in_area(math_addition, "F2", "F5", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(Write(math_addition))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Conclusion
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Visual emphasis on the resultant vector
        self.play(Flash(res_vec, color=COLOR_RESULTANT, line_length=0.3, flash_radius=0.4))
        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Adding vectors is like following sequential instructions.",
            "Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.",
            "The result is the arrow from start to end.",
            "Numerically, we simply add the corresponding components.",
            "This new vector represents the combined total movement."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_PLANE = "#1E90FF"
        COLOR_WIND = "#FF00FF"
        COLOR_RESULTANT = "#FFFF00"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = YELLOW

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Introductory line
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR))
        self.wait(1.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw Plane and Wind vectors
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_WIND)
        )
        
        # Positions
        plane_start = self.grid["D2"]
        plane_end = self.grid["D4"]
        wind_start = plane_end
        wind_end = self.grid["B4"]
        
        # Plane Vector
        plane_vec = Arrow(plane_start, plane_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_PLANE)
        plane_label = Text("Plane", font_size=20, color=COLOR_PLANE)

            new_arrow = plane.get_vector([k * 1, k * 2], color=VECTOR_COLOR)
            m.become(new_arrow)
            
        v_arrow.add_updater(update_arrow)

        self.wait(1)

        # "Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar flipping to -1
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(-1.0), run_time=2.0)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "This scaling is the core of linear transformations."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(VECTOR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar to 3.0 as specified in storyboard [3, 6]
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(3.0), run_time=2.0)
        
        # Final result mathematical formula
        final_res_math = MathTex(r"3 \cdot \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(final_res_math, "A4", scale_factor=0.9)

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Section Title and Lecture Lines
        title_text = "Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors.",
            "Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks the arrow.",
            "A scalar of two doubles the vector's length.",
            "Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction.",
            "This scaling is the core of linear transformations."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Color Constants
        VECTOR_COLOR = "#ADFF2F"  # Greenish
        SCALAR_COLOR = "#FFD700"  # Gold
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR))
        
        # Mathematical representation of the initial vector
        vec_v_math = MathTex(r"\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(vec_v_math, "A3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Create a coordinate system (NumberPlane) to visualize vectors
        # Fitting within area B3 to F6 (roughly 3x4 grid units)
        plane = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-4, 4, 1],
            y_range=[-7, 7, 1],
            x_length=3.5,
            y_length=4.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": True, "stroke_width": 1.5, "color": GREY},
            background_line_style={"stroke_opacity": 0.2}
        )
        self.place_in_area(plane, "B3", "F6")
        
        # The vector mobject
        v_arrow = plane.get_vector([1, 2], color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        v_label = MathTex(r"\vec{v}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        
        # Label updater to stay near the arrow tip
        def update_label(m):
            end_pos = v_arrow.get_end()
            # Dynamic placement to avoid overlapping the origin/axis
            direction = UR if end_pos[1] >= plane.get_origin()[1] else DL
            m.next_to(end_pos, direction, buff=0.1)
        
        v_label.add_updater(update_label)

        self.play(Write(vec_v_math))
        self.play(Create(plane))
        self.play(GrowArrow(v_arrow), FadeIn(v_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks the arrow."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Scalar tracker for smooth animation
        k_tracker = ValueTracker(1.0)
        
        # Scalar variable display (using DecimalNumber for performance)
        scalar_label = MathTex("k =", color=SCALAR_COLOR)
        scalar_val = DecimalNumber(1.0, color=SCALAR_COLOR, num_decimal_places=1)
        scalar_val.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_value(k_tracker.get_value()))
        scalar_group = VGroup(scalar_label, scalar_val).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(scalar_group, "A5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Result expression k*v placeholder
        res_math = MathTex(r"k \cdot \vec{v}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(res_math, "A4", scale_factor=0.9)
        
        # Updater to scale the vector arrow geometry based on k
        def update_arrow(m):
            k = k_tracker.get_value()
            new_arrow = plane.get_vector([k * 1, k * 2], color=VECTOR_COLOR)
            m.become(new_arrow)
            
        v_arrow.add_updater(update_arrow)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(scalar_group), Write(res_math))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "A scalar of two doubles the vector's length."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar growing to 2
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(2.0), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # "Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar flipping to -1
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(-1.0), run_time=2.0)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "This scaling is the core of linear transformations."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(VECTOR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar to 3.0 as specified in storyboard [3, 6]
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(3.0), run_time=2.0)
        
        # Final result mathematical formula
        final_res_math = MathTex(r"3 \cdot \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(final_res_math, "A4", scale_factor=0.9)
        
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(res_math, final_res_math))
        self.wait(2)

        # Cleanup updaters to avoid runtime overhead after animation
        v_arrow.remove_updater(update_arrow)
        v_label.remove_updater(update_label)
        scalar_val.clear_updaters()

section_1.title: Prerequisite: From Points to Directions
section_1.content: Briefly revisit the Cartesian coordinate system. Distinguish between a 'point' (a static location) and a 'vector' (an instruction for movement). Explain that while a point is a destination, a vector is the journey.
section_1.example: Imagine a cat sitting at coordinate (0,0). To get to a bowl of milk at (3,2), the cat must move 3 units right and 2 units up. That specific instruction—the movement itself—is our vector.

section_2.title: The Geometry of a Vector
section_2.content: Introduce the visual representation of a vector as an arrow in space. Emphasize two critical properties: Magnitude (length of the arrow) and Direction (where it points). Explain that vectors can slide around the graph as long as length and angle remain the same.
section_2.example: Visualize a gust of wind represented by an arrow. Whether the wind blows at the park or the beach, if it's 20mph heading North-East, it's the same vector.

section_3.title: The Algebra of Vectors: The 'Recipe'
section_3.content: Translate the visual arrow into a numerical list (a column matrix). Explain the [x, y] notation as a 'recipe' for movement. Show how the vector [3, -2] translates to '3 steps forward, 2 steps down' on the grid.
section_3.example: A game character 'Hero_A' has a movement vector of [4, 1]. In an animation, we show a ghost overlay of the hero moving 4 units along the x-axis and 1 unit up the y-axis to reach their new position.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_4.content: Demonstrate how to combine two vectors. Visually, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Numerically, show that we simply add the corresponding x and y components.
section_4.example: A plane is flying with a velocity vector [10, 0] (moving straight East). A crosswind hits it with a vector [0, 2] (moving North). The resulting path of the plane is the diagonal arrow formed by [10+0, 0+2] = [10, 2].

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World
section_5.content: Introduce 'Scalars' (regular numbers). Show how multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches, shrinks, or flips the direction (if the scalar is negative). This is the 'linear' part of linear algebra.
section_5.example: If a rocket's thrust vector is [1, 2], and we activate 'Turbo Mode' (a scalar of 3), the new vector becomes [3, 6]. Visually, the arrow grows three times longer but maintains the same slope.

section_6.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_6.content: Summarize how vectors serve as the building blocks for computer graphics, physics engines, and data science. Reiterate that a vector is both a geometric arrow and a list of numbers.
section_6.example: Show a quick montage: a 3D character model made of thousands of vectors, a weather map of wind velocities, and a search engine ranking results based on 'vector similarity'.

outline.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
outline.content: Demonstrate how to combine two vectors. Visually, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Numerically, show that we simply add the corresponding x and y components.
outline.example: A plane is flying with a velocity vector [10, 0] (moving straight East). A crosswind hits it with a vector [0, 2] (moving North). The resulting path of the plane is the diagonal arrow formed by [10+0, 0+2] = [10, 2].

storyboard.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
lecture_lines: Adding vectors is like following sequential instructions.
Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.
The result is the arrow from start to end.
Numerically, we simply add the corresponding components.
This new vector represents the combined total movement.
animations: Draw a #1E90FF vector labeled 'A' starting from origin.
Place a #FF00FF vector 'B' at 'A's tip.
Draw a #FFFF00 vector from origin to 'B's tip.
Display addition: [x1+x2, y1+y2] in #FFFFFF near the vectors.
Flash the #FFFF00 resultant vector to show total movement.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Adding vectors is like following sequential instructions.",
            "Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.",
            "The result is the arrow from start to end.",
            "Numerically, we simply add the corresponding components.",
            "This new vector represents the combined total movement."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_PLANE = "#1E90FF"
        COLOR_WIND = "#FF00FF"
        COLOR_RESULTANT = "#FFFF00"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = YELLOW

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Introductory line
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR))
        self.wait(1.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw Plane and Wind vectors
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_WIND)
        )
        
        # Positions
        plane_start = self.grid["D2"]
        plane_end = self.grid["D4"]
        wind_start = plane_end
        wind_end = self.grid["B4"]
        
        # Plane Vector
        plane_vec = Arrow(plane_start, plane_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_PLANE)
        plane_label = Text("Plane", font_size=20, color=COLOR_PLANE)
        self.place_at_grid(plane_label, "E3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Wind Vector
        wind_vec = Arrow(wind_start, wind_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_WIND)
        wind_label = Text("Wind", font_size=20, color=COLOR_WIND)
        self.place_at_grid(wind_label, "C5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(plane_vec), Write(plane_label))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(Create(wind_vec), Write(wind_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Draw Resultant vector
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_RESULTANT)
        )
        
        res_vec = Arrow(plane_start, wind_end, buff=0, color=COLOR_RESULTANT)
        res_label = Text("Resultant", font_size=20, color=COLOR_RESULTANT)
        self.place_at_grid(res_label, "C2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(res_vec), Write(res_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Numerical addition

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Section Title and Lecture Lines
        title_text = "Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the World"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors.",
            "Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks the arrow.",
            "A scalar of two doubles the vector's length.",
            "Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction.",
            "This scaling is the core of linear transformations."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Color Constants
        VECTOR_COLOR = "#ADFF2F"  # Greenish
        SCALAR_COLOR = "#FFD700"  # Gold
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR))
        
        # Mathematical representation of the initial vector
        vec_v_math = MathTex(r"\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(vec_v_math, "A3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Create a coordinate system (NumberPlane) to visualize vectors
        # Fitting within area B3 to F6 (roughly 3x4 grid units)
        plane = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-4, 4, 1],
            y_range=[-7, 7, 1],
            x_length=3.5,
            y_length=4.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": True, "stroke_width": 1.5, "color": GREY},
            background_line_style={"stroke_opacity": 0.2}
        )
        self.place_in_area(plane, "B3", "F6")
        
        # The vector mobject
        v_arrow = plane.get_vector([1, 2], color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        v_label = MathTex(r"\vec{v}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        
        # Label updater to stay near the arrow tip
        def update_label(m):
            end_pos = v_arrow.get_end()
            # Dynamic placement to avoid overlapping the origin/axis
            direction = UR if end_pos[1] >= plane.get_origin()[1] else DL
            m.next_to(end_pos, direction, buff=0.1)
        
        v_label.add_updater(update_label)

        self.play(Write(vec_v_math))
        self.play(Create(plane))
        self.play(GrowArrow(v_arrow), FadeIn(v_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks the arrow."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Scalar tracker for smooth animation
        k_tracker = ValueTracker(1.0)
        
        # Scalar variable display (using DecimalNumber for performance)
        scalar_label = MathTex("k =", color=SCALAR_COLOR)
        scalar_val = DecimalNumber(1.0, color=SCALAR_COLOR, num_decimal_places=1)
        scalar_val.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_value(k_tracker.get_value()))
        scalar_group = VGroup(scalar_label, scalar_val).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(scalar_group, "A5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Result expression k*v placeholder
        res_math = MathTex(r"k \cdot \vec{v}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(res_math, "A4", scale_factor=0.9)
        
        # Updater to scale the vector arrow geometry based on k
        def update_arrow(m):
            k = k_tracker.get_value()
            new_arrow = plane.get_vector([k * 1, k * 2], color=VECTOR_COLOR)
            m.become(new_arrow)
            
        v_arrow.add_updater(update_arrow)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(scalar_group), Write(res_math))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "A scalar of two doubles the vector's length."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar growing to 2
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(2.0), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # "Negative scalars flip the vector to the opposite direction."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(SCALAR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar flipping to -1
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(-1.0), run_time=2.0)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "This scaling is the core of linear transformations."
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(VECTOR_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Animate scalar to 3.0 as specified in storyboard [3, 6]
        self.play(k_tracker.animate.set_value(3.0), run_time=2.0)
        
        # Final result mathematical formula
        final_res_math = MathTex(r"3 \cdot \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}", color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(final_res_math, "A4", scale_factor=0.9)
        
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(res_math, final_res_math))
        self.wait(2)

        # Cleanup updaters to avoid runtime overhead after animation
        v_arrow.remove_updater(update_arrow)
        v_label.remove_updater(update_label)
        scalar_val.clear_updaters()
